rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html Theorem 6.4 (Ville) and proof, lines 281-294
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-derived step by step. B_k = {M_j < h for all j <= k}, B_{−1} = Ω, A_k = B_{k−1} \ B_k; the A_k are disjoint, their union is {max_{k<=n} M_k >= h}, and A_k, B_k are functions of Y_1..Y_k. For W_n = Σ_{k<=n} M_k·1_{A_k} + M_n·1_{B_n}, A_n ∪ B_n = B_{n−1} (disjoint) gives W_n − W_{n−1} = (M_n − M_{n−1})·1_{B_{n−1}}. Taking out what is known gives E_0[W_n − W_{n−1}] = E_0[1_{B_{n−1}}(E_0[M_n|past] − M_{n−1})] <= 0, with integrability from E_0[M_t] <= 1, and W_0 = M_0 = 1. W_n >= h·1{max >= h}, so P(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) <= 1/h; then continuity from below; then the h' < h argument extends the bound to {sup >= h}. Complete, and it needs no optional-stopping theorem (M6). The supermartingale version generalizes the cited test-martingale Eq. (8) and is proved on the page.

rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-derived from scratch (line 440 changed). With A_n the event that some look among the first n rejects (Proposition 6.1), A_n is contained in A_{n+1}, so an added look can only add rejections, with extra probability P(A_{n+1} minus A_n). For normal data that difference contains the open set {|S_t| < b_t for t <= n, |S_{n+1}| > b_{n+1}} for any finite positive boundaries b_t: it is nonempty (y_1 = ... = y_n = 0, y_{n+1} = 2 b_{n+1}) and the density of (Y_1, ..., Y_{n+1}) is positive everywhere, so the probability is positive. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html Lab 4 interpretation, line 422, the derivation after the T span
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: New displayed result since 9b6be31, re-derived. Claim: with h = 1/alpha, h P0(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) + E0[sum_{k<=n} (M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] <= 1. Derivation: Theorem 6.4's proof gives E0[W_n] <= 1 with W_n = sum_k M_k 1_{A_k} + M_n 1_{B_n}; drop the nonnegative term M_n 1_{B_n} and write M_k = h + (M_k - h) on A_k. Sound. Second claim: the expected overshoot O_n = E0[sum_{k<=n}(M_k - h) 1_{A_k}] is nondecreasing in n because every summand is >= 0 (M_k >= h on A_k); it is positive from the first day n_0 with P(A_{n_0}) > 0 because M_{n_0} > h almost surely on A_{n_0} (shown in the previous sentence for the monitor); so P(max_{k<=n} M_k >= h) <= (1 - O_n)/h = alpha (1 - O_n) <= alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) for n >= n_0, and letting n grow (monotone limit) the probability of ever crossing is at most alpha (1 - O_{n_0}) < alpha. Sound; for this monitor n_0 = 1 and the gap is tiny in absolute terms but strictly positive, and the sentence claims only 'strictly below alpha'. Numerical spot-check (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify8-L01-L02/overshoot.py, 40,000 null paths of the monitor with alpha = 0.05, kappa = 252, horizon 2520): P(cross) = 0.0199 < 0.05, E[overshoot] = 0.0191 > 0, h P + O = 0.417 <= E[W_n] = 0.989 <= 1. Notation: h, M_k, A_k, B_k and 'the same steps' refer to the proof of Theorem 6.4, which the sentence names; A_n of Proposition 6.1's proof is a different, proof-local event, so there is no collision inside either proof. The displayed derivation is on-page (T by proof); it is not wrapped in a claim span, as is usual for derived interpretation text.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L01.html Remark 6.9, paragraph 2, line 440, first two sentences
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Round-8 FAIL, re-checked from scratch at 3dd9a69 (line 440 changed in 9a7195b). The page now reads: 'Within its budget a group-sequential design with a fixed number of looks can be cheap, as O'Brien and Fleming's power finding above illustrates. A spending design's guarantee also ends with its budget, though.' This is exactly the round-8 proposed replacement. Re-judged on its own merits. (1) Support: the evidence for 'can be cheap' is the B span on line 439 (O'Brien and Fleming, Abstract). I re-read the abstract (OpenAlex, curl 2026-10-19, no email, /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-quant-phd/cdd15252-4236-59f9-8fa8-e63e41e1dc0d/scratchpad/verify9-L01-L02/dl/oa_10_2307_2530245.json): 'comparing two treatments when response to treatment is both dichotomous ... and immediate ... The maximum number (N) of tests and the number (m1 + m2) of observations collected between successive tests is fixed in advance. The overall size of the procedure is shown to be controlled with virtually the same accuracy as the single sample chi-square test ... The power is also found to be virtually the same.' That is a fixed-number-of-looks design, so a power finding about it supports a statement about 'a group-sequential design with a fixed number of looks', and 'can be cheap' is existential and says 'illustrates', not 'all such designs are'. (2) The second sentence moved to 'a spending design' (Lan and DeMets); its support is not the O'Brien-Fleming finding but the page's own argument two sentences later (nested events as in Proposition 6.1, positive probability by part (b), so a design that has spent all of alpha exceeds alpha once an uncovered look is added), which I re-derived (see L01-math-rem69-extralook). The Lan-DeMets abstract (OpenAlex, same date, dl/oa_10_1093_biomet_70_3_659.json) says the boundary 'is determined by alpha*(t), and by past and current decision times, but does not depend on the future decision times or the total number of decision times': a spending design is flexible about the number and timing of looks inside its budget and has no alpha left beyond it, which is what 'ends with its budget' says. (3) Consistency with the rest of the page, re-read: line 439 ('Pocock ... O'Brien and Fleming fix the maximum number of tests ... Lan and DeMets ... replace it with a function alpha*(t)'), quiz item 14's explanation ('Pocock and O'Brien-Fleming fix the number of looks in advance; Lan and DeMets free their number and timing but still spend a fixed alpha'), key-results row 13 and card S7-c146 all separate fixed-look designs from spending designs the same way. The generalization from a fixed-look design's power to 'a spending design' is gone.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'A false rejection' (lines 443-445)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-derived. Almost surely every q_j > 0 (q_j = 0 only for one value of U), so the i - 1 zeros are p_(1) = ... = p_(i-1) = 0 and p_(i) = min_j q_j belongs to a true null. Zeros pass steps 1, ..., i - 1 because the constants are positive (the step fails only when p_(k) > c_k). If min_j q_j <= c <= c_i, step i passes, so the first failing index is > i and H_(i), a true null, is rejected. Hence FWER >= P(min q <= c) = m'c = min(m' c_i, 1) > alpha (m' c_i > alpha by hypothesis, 1 > alpha). The page states it as an inequality; the equality FWER = min(m' c_i, 1) also holds (step i is then decisive: it passes iff min q <= c_i, and the arcs of length c_i cover the circle when c_i >= 1/m'), which I confirmed numerically; the lesson does not need it. [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, part (a) (line 446)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-derived and simulated. With c_i = alpha/m', c = alpha/m' (<= 1/m' because alpha < 1). If p_(i) = min q > alpha/m' step i fails with steps 1..i-1 passed, so only the i - 1 false nulls are rejected and V = 0; if min q <= alpha/m', H_(i) is rejected, V >= 1. Hence FWER = m' (alpha/m') = alpha, for every i = 1..m, i.e. m' = m..1 true nulls. The closing sentence ('Every inequality in the proof of Theorem 3.2 holds with equality here') checked line by line against Theorem 3.2's proof: j <= m - m_0 + 1 is an equality (j = i = m - m' + 1); alpha/(m + 1 - j) <= alpha/m_0 is an equality (m + 1 - j = m'); {V >= 1} contained in {min <= alpha/m_0} is an equality of events (just shown); Boole's inequality is an equality (disjoint events); validity is an equality (uniform). Numerical: for m = 1..8 and every i the exact-grid FWER of Holm under the construction is 0.05 to machine precision (max |FWER - 0.05| = 0). [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.] [round-16 addition: 'Boole's inequality is an equality (disjoint events)': the equality needs only null pairwise overlaps, i.e. events disjoint up to a null set. The page's wording at line 441 and line 446 is FAIL in L02-math-P4-disjoint.]

Raising c_2 to 0.03 > 0.025: m' = 2, c = min(0.03, 0.5) = 0.03; p_1 = 0, p_2 = U, p_3 = (U + 1/2) mod 1; {p_2 <= 0.03} = {U <= 0.03}, {p_3 <= 0.03} = {0.5 <= U <= 0.53}, disjoint, P = 0.06 > 0.05. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'Zeros are a convenience' (line 448)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-derived. False-null p-values in (0, delta] with delta <= c_j for all j < i: on {delta < min_j q_j <= c} the i - 1 smallest p-values are the false nulls' (each <= delta <= its constant, so steps 1..i-1 pass) and p_(i) = min q <= c <= c_i passes, so a true null is rejected. For delta <= c, P(delta < min q <= c) = m'(c - delta) because the arcs of length delta (<= c <= 1/m') are also disjoint; it exceeds alpha iff delta < c - alpha/m'. The claim is a lower bound on the FWER, as written ('exceeds alpha once delta < c - alpha/m''). Simulated (400 random cases, random m <= 8, random i, random other constants, random false-null p-values in (0, delta]): the estimated FWER was never below m'(c - delta) - 1e-3 and was above alpha whenever delta < c - alpha/m' - 1e-3 (0 violations). [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.] [round-16 addition: the arcs of length delta meet at endpoints when delta = c = 1/m'; the identity Prob(min q <= c) - Prob(min q <= delta) = m'(c - delta) holds because the overlaps are null sets, so the row's probability claim stands; 'disjoint' in this row means disjoint up to a null set (see L02-math-P4-disjoint).]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P4 solution, 'What it shows' (line 449)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Checked sentence by sentence. (1) 'A step-down procedure with fixed constants that controls the FWER at level alpha under every joint distribution of valid p-values must have c_k <= alpha/(m + 1 - k) for every k': the contrapositive of the main result (positive constants, alpha < 1). (2) 'Raising constants only adds rejections, because the first failure moves later, so Holm's procedure rejects everything such a procedure rejects, for every vector of p-values': if c_k <= Holm_k for all k then p_(k) > Holm_k implies p_(k) > c_k, so the first failing index of the c-procedure is no later than Holm's and it rejects a subset. (3) 'A gain beyond Holm's needs the dependence between the tests (Lessons 4 and 5)': true for the class the problem treats (p-value step-down with fixed constants, every configuration of true nulls possible, only marginal validity). Outside that class gains can come from logical relations between the hypotheses (Shaffer 1986) as well as from dependence; the sentence is a pointer, sits after the sentence that fixes the class, and is not a graded claim span. Note, not a failure. (4) The T span after it matches Lehmann and Romano Theorem 2.3(ii) (L02-cite-lehmann2005generalizations). [git diff 202ea24..50d202e changes course/modules/S/S7/L02.html at line 88 only (the fwer-growth caption); the passage of this row is outside that line.]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c187 (lesson L02, grade T); course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Proposition 3.3 (lines 196-204)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Re-checked from scratch. Proposition 3.3 (L02.html 196-204): 'For any p-values, every hypothesis rejected by the Bonferroni correction at level α is rejected by Holm's procedure at level α.' Its proof: 'Suppose Bonferroni rejects H_(b), so p_(b) ≤ α/m. For every b' ≤ b, p_(b') ≤ p_(b) ≤ α/m ≤ α/(m+1−b'), because m+1−b' ≤ m. So Holm passes steps 1..b, and its first failure, if any, comes after b. Hence Holm rejects H_(b).' Card back: 'Yes (Proposition 3.3). If Bonferroni rejects H_(b), then p_(b) ≤ α/m, and for every b' ≤ b, p_(b') ≤ p_(b) ≤ α/m ≤ α/(m + 1 − b'), so Holm passes steps 1 to b and rejects H_(b).' The card is the proof's core step and the statement's conclusion, one fact, correct, grade T (proved on the page, no cite needed; cf. S7-c002). Numerical check (scratch scripts/card_numbers.py, python -I, numpy): 48,000 random p-vectors for m = 1..12 with mixed small and large p-values at α = 0.05: 71,294 Bonferroni rejections, and 0 cases in which Bonferroni rejects a hypothesis Holm does not. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 88 (new figcaption sentence)
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: New sentence: 'testing each hypothesis at α/m holds the family-wise error rate at or below α for every m, and here, with independent nulls, at exactly α only when m = 1.' Derivation: by Boole's inequality (as in the proof of Theorem 2.2), the FWER of m true nulls each tested at α/m is at most m·(α/m) = α for any dependence, so 'at or below α for every m' holds. With independent true nulls, FWER = 1 − (1 − α/m)^m. Bernoulli's inequality (1 − x)^m ≥ 1 − mx holds with strict inequality for m ≥ 2 and 0 < x < 1, so FWER < α for m ≥ 2; at m = 1 the FWER is exactly α. Numerical check (scratch scripts/card_numbers.py, python -I, .venv): for α = 0.01..0.10 and m = 1..200, 500, 1000, 5000: 0 violations of FWER ≤ α; strictly below α for every m ≥ 2; |FWER − α| ≤ 1e-15 at m = 1. Values: α = 0.05: FWER(2) = 0.049375, FWER(1000) = 0.048772; α = 0.01: FWER(1000) = 0.009950. The figure's readout and desc in every state agree (row L02-fig-fwer-growth). [round-16 addition: caption (line 88) unchanged; claims re-checked over all alpha states at 535fd80 (caption_checks_535fd80.out).]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Remark 3.5 claim span (line 272, data-cite romano2005stepwise) and key-results row 8 (line 530); the counter-evidence search for the grade B
rows.evidence: unchanged since 2aa80db (git diff checked); round-15 evidence: Method (round 12, 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-20). Question: does any published work contest the claim that the Romano-Wolf stepwise bootstrap controls the FWER asymptotically with more power than single-step methods (L02 Remark 3.5 and key-results row 8)? Sources, each fetched this round with a User-Agent header only (no e-mail, no mailto, no key). (1) OpenCitations index v2, https://api.opencitations.net/index/v2/citations/doi:10.1111/j.1468-0262.2005.00615.x: 711 citing rows; 708 distinct citing DOIs; 3 rows are arXiv IDs only (1812.04345, 2103.09603, 2107.10017). (2) Crossref work records for the 708 DOIs: 707 resolved; 1 DataCite dataset DOI (10.4225/03/5935ff87c8d5c) returned 404; 298 carry an abstract. The RW record has is-referenced-by-count 770, so about 60 Crossref-counted citers are outside OpenCitations; Crossref has no citers filter (reference.doi and reference-doi are rejected with HTTP 400), so those were not screened. (3) OpenAlex cites filter for W3123939061: HTTP 429 until the daily reset at 00:00 UTC, then HTTP 200 with count 1013 (pages 1 to 6 by offset; cursor paging needs a key, which was not requested): 972 with a DOI (968 distinct), of which 658 are in the OpenCitations set and 310 are OpenAlex-only; 607 carry an abstract. (4) Screens: title or abstract matches the key set (multiple testing, power, Romano, Wolf, step-down, stepwise, Holm, Bonferroni, FWER, single-step, StepM, reality check): 159 of 707 Crossref records and 178 of 1013 OpenAlex works. Contest set (Romano, Wolf, step-down, stepwise, Holm, Bonferroni, family-wise, FWER, single-step, StepM, reality check) in title or abstract: 39 Crossref records; 13 further OpenCitations records through OpenAlex abstracts (for 151 of the 409 records without a Crossref abstract); 16 OpenAlex-only works. (5) Contest-set records without a Crossref abstract were checked against OpenAlex (13 of them have one, read in (4)). The rest were screened by title and venue: applications (Empirical Economics 2015; Decision Support Systems 2010); method papers whose titles make no power claim about Romano-Wolf (Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 2014; Statistics and Probability Letters 2016 twice; SSRN 2016); and the JFEC 2014 record, whose publisher abstract is read in (6) from OpenAlex. 258 of the 409 records without a Crossref abstract have no abstract in either source and were screened by title only. (6) Abstracts and texts read, with verdicts. Hansen (2005, SSRN 264569; JBES 2005): the SPA test is more powerful than White's single-step Reality Check; not about Romano-Wolf; no contest. Hsu, Hsu and Kuan (SSRN 1087044; JEF 2010, doi 10.1016/j.jempfin.2010.01.001): the stepwise SPA test 'is more powerful than the stepwise Reality Check test of Romano and Wolf (2005)'; a stepwise-versus-stepwise comparison; no contest (the JEF page returned a captcha, so the SSRN abstract was read). Hsu, Kuan and Yen (JFEC 2014, doi 10.1093/jjfinec/nbu014; abstract from the OpenAlex journal record): Step-SPA(k) is 'more powerful than Step-RC(k) under any power notion defined in Romano and Wolf (2005)'; no single-step comparison; no contest (the Oxford University Press page is a Cloudflare challenge, HTTP 403). Market-timing rule performance (JFEC 2011, doi 10.1093/jjfinec/nbq032): applies the RC, SPA and stepwise tests; no RW-versus-single-step comparison; no contest. Survey expectations and adjustments for multiple testing (JEBO 2024): 'The Bonferroni correction and related approaches ... are conservative and result in low power when the null hypotheses are false'; supports the page's comparison; not a contest. Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics (2023, doi 10.3389/fams.2023.1151314; full text read): 'in all scenarios we considered, Romano and Wolf's method uniformly outperformed methods other than the one we propose' (Bonferroni, Holm, minP and Westfall-Young step-down among them); corroborates. Clarke, Romano and Wolf (2020, Stata Journal, doi 10.1177/1536867x20976314; PDF read): the correction is 'considerably more powerful than earlier multiple-testing procedures, such as the Bonferroni and Holm corrections'; corroborates. arXiv 2107.10017 (2021 preprint on cluster-randomised trials; abstract read): 'the Romano-Wolf type procedure ... is more efficient than the other methods in a simulation-based study'; corroborates (preprint). Harvey and Liu, 'False (and Missed) Discoveries in Financial Economics' (arXiv 2006.04269, 2020; abstract read): 'Evaluating current methods, we find that they lack power to detect outperforming managers'; a general claim about current methods with no RW-versus-single-step comparison in the abstract; not a contest as scoped; the Journal of Finance full text was not read. Harvey and Liu's evaluation for finance (RAPS 2020, doi 10.1093/rapstu/raaa003): the abstract states no finding; the full text is behind an OUP challenge (HTTP 403); not read. Extended MinP tests (arXiv 1911.04696; Econometric Reviews 2026): combination tests; no RW power claim. Testing many moment inequalities (WP 2013): Bonferroni and multiplier-bootstrap critical values; no RW comparison in the abstract. The Stepwise Cauchy Combination Test (JFEC 2025, doi 10.1093/jjfinec/nbaf020; Crossref abstract): 'more powerful than conventional multiple testing corrections'; a newer competitor, not a contest of Romano-Wolf against single-step methods (freshness flag). (7) Result: no contest found in any screened source. Limits, stated plainly: about 60 Crossref-counted citers are not in the OpenCitations list and were not screened; 258 records have no abstract; the RAPS 2020 full text and the Econometrica, JFEC 2014 and JEF 2010 publisher pages were not readable (HTTP 403 or captcha). These limits are recorded in the registry flags. [round-16 addition: re-run at 535fd80 (OpenCitations 711 rows; Crossref search rerun, 25 rows, see counter_targets_r16_535fd80.out): see L01-L02-counter-romano2005stepwise-535fd80.]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 129 (the paragraph after Example 2.4)
rows.evidence: Re-checked from scratch at 535fd80. git diff 2aa80db 535fd80 -- L02.html has one hunk at line 129 (two sentences changed). The paragraph now reads: 'The bound in (1) is attained when the true-null p-values are uniform and their rejection events {p_i <= alpha/m} are pairwise disjoint (Problem P2), and it becomes loose when those events overlap with positive probability. In the extreme where all null p-values are one uniform variable, the union of m0 identical events is one event, and Bonferroni's FWER is alpha/m, not alpha. Correlation alone does not decide where between these extremes a family falls: Problem P2 shows that events disjoint up to a null set can come from positively correlated p-values. The next lab measures how the family-wise error rate of equicorrelated Gaussian statistics falls as their correlation rises.' Claims: (1) attained when uniform and pairwise disjoint: TRUE as a sufficient condition (P(V>=1) = sum P(A_i) = m0 alpha/m; p2_recheck_535fd80.out sections 2 and 6). (2) loose when the events overlap with positive probability: TRUE. Pointwise 1{union A_i} <= sum_i 1{A_i} - 1{A1 and A2} gives P(union) <= sum P(A_i) - P(A1 n A2) < m0 alpha/m (section 6: 3000 random finite spaces, 0 violations; section 5: intersection 0.015006 and union 0.035006 for shift 1/100, threshold 1/40, against m0 alpha/m = 0.05). (3) identical events give alpha/m: TRUE. (4) P2 shows events disjoint up to a null set from positively correlated p-values: TRUE (section 2: A1 n A2 = {0} on the exact grid; section 1: corr = 683/800 = 0.85375 > 0). (5) the next lab measures FWER falling as correlation rises: TRUE (Lab 1 output at 535fd80: Bonferroni 0.0491, 0.0287, 0.0056 for rho = 0, 0.5, 0.9; lab_check_535fd80.out). Neighbouring text checked and consistent: Remark 3.5 (conservatism scoped to equicorrelated Gaussian statistics), line 165 (Lab 1 interpretation), quiz item 8 (scoped to Lab 1), the P2 last sentence ('a positive correlation does not by itself make Bonferroni conservative'), card S7-c231 (sufficient condition). Round-15 FAIL resolved.

rows.evidence: Re-checked at 535fd80 as a neighbour of the changed line 129. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421, the shifted construction
rows.evidence: Re-derived at 535fd80 with s = alpha/2 and p2 = (U + s) mod 1. For U in [0, 1 - s): p2 = U + s > s, so p2 <= s only at U = 0 (p2 = s). For U in [1 - s, 1): p2 = U + s - 1 in [0, s), so p2 <= s. Hence {p2 <= s} = {0} u [1 - s, 1) (exact on the 160000-point rational grid: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 2, 'A2 equals {0} u [1 - alpha/2, 1) on the grid: True'). Since s < 1 - s for alpha < 1, {U <= s} n {p2 <= s} = {0}, a null set. P(A1) = P(A2) = s, P(A1 n A2) = 0, so P(union) = 2s = alpha. The text 'which meets {U <= alpha/2} only at the null point U = 0, so the two events are disjoint up to a null set and the FWER is again exactly alpha' is TRUE. Monte Carlo: section 3 (mean over 20 seeds of 1,000,000 draws: 0.050002 +- 0.000035). Round-15 FAIL (L02-math-P2-shift-disjoint PASS in round 15) re-checked and still PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html Problem P2 solution, line 421 ('E[U((U+s) mod 1)] = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 ... correlation 1 - 6s(1-s)')
rows.evidence: Derivation at 535fd80. V = (U + s) mod 1 equals U + s on [0, 1-s) and U + s - 1 on [1-s, 1]. E[UV] = int_0^{1-s} u(u+s) du + int_{1-s}^1 u(u+s-1) du = [(1-s)^3/3 + s(1-s)^2/2] + [1/3 - (1-s)/2 + (1-s)^3/6] = (1-s)^2/2 + 1/3 - (1-s)/2 = 1/3 - s(1-s)/2 (using (1-s)^3/2 + s(1-s)^2/2 = (1-s)^2/2 and (1-s)^2/2 - (1-s)/2 = -s(1-s)/2). With E U = E V = 1/2 and Var U = Var V = 1/12 (V uniform), Cov = 1/12 - s(1-s)/2 and corr = 12 Cov = 1 - 6s(1-s). Numerical check: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 1 evaluates both identities with Fraction arithmetic at 28 rational shifts (k/13, k/97, 1/2, 1/40, 1/20, 1/10, 3/7, 1/4, 2/9, 7/11): both hold exactly at every point (printed: 'points tested: 28'). E[UV] and corr are polynomials of degree at most 3 in s, so 28 exact agreements cover the family. PASS.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L02.html line 129, clause 'and it becomes loose when those events overlap with positive probability'
rows.evidence: Re-checked at 535fd80. Claim: with overlap of positive probability the bound is strictly loose. Proof: for indicators, 1{union A_i} <= sum_i 1{A_i} - 1{A_1 n A_2} pointwise (k = number of events containing the point: k = 0 and k = 1 give equality, k >= 2 gives k - 1 >= 1). Taking expectations, P(union) <= sum P(A_i) - P(A_1 n A_2). With validity P(A_i) <= alpha/m, P(A_1 n A_2) > 0 gives P(V>=1) < m0 alpha/m: strictly loose. Checks: p2_recheck_535fd80.out section 6 (3000 random finite probability spaces with 3 to 6 events and Fraction weights: 0 violations; 0 cases with overlap in which the plain union bound sum P(A_i) is attained) and section 5 (concrete partial overlap: FWER 0.035006 < 0.05 = m0 alpha/m). The round-15 counterexample (the shifted P2 events meeting only in {0}) has probability-zero overlap, so the bound is attained there, and the corrected sentence says 'with positive probability' precisely to exclude it (section 2: intersection {0}). Round-15 FAIL resolved.
